SII_notes: This records an endowment of land, one vēli in extent, as tax-free dēvadāna for the requirements of daily offerings and worship and a perpetual lamp in the temple of Paramēśvara at Tiruppaḻuvūr in Viḷattūr-nāḍu, by Mahimālaiya Irukkuvēḷ alias Parāntakaṉ Vīraśōḻaṉ. The donor seems to have belonged to the family of Irukkuvēḷs of Koḍumbāḷūr figuring in the Pudukkōṭṭai inscriptions, and should have been a feudal chief under Parāntaka I or II. The Rājakēsari of this inscription might therefore refer to Gaṇḍarāditya or Sundara-Chōḷa. Since however, the record mentions a lunar eclipse in the month of Kanyā—one occurred in A.D. 954 (September 15) and another in A.D. 955 (September 4)—it is more probably that of the former.

SII_translation:
Hail Prosperity! In the 5th year of king Rājakesarivarman, on the day of the solar eclipse occurring in the month of Kaṉṉi, Mahimālaya Irukkuveḷ also called Parāntakan Viracoḻaṉ made a gift of land made pure by pouring water, to endure as long as the moon and the sun last, to the paramēśvara of Paḻuvūr in Viḷattūr nāṭu.

The land given is one veli of land, plus half and half-māvu of cennatai-ppuṟam of the old temple (tevatāṉam) of this Paḻuvūr, making a total land of one and a half and half-māvu.

SII_translation:
Hail Prosperity! In the thirteenth year of Kopparakesarivarman, Cempaṉ Aruḷan, known as Nuttamaniti and Uttamacoḻa-muventaveḷār, built the stone temple (tirukkaṟṟaḷi) for the Mahādevar of Tiruveḷḷaṭai in Tiruvāli-nāṭu, and established the sacred drums (śrīpali-koṭṭu) for this god.

The persons bound to beat the drums are nine in number:
Three persons led by Śrītaraṉ, known as Pāṅkāṇai, the Añūṟṟuva-veḷāṉ of this village;
Four persons led by Uttamanitip Perukaccaṉ, who is Kāṭan, son of Mātarcivaṉ Māṇikkaṉ of Kaḻanivāyil in Tiruvaḻuntūr-nāṭu, having received strītaṉam by marrying the daughter of the aforesaid Añūṟṟuva-veḷāṉ;
And two persons on the days... having also received strīta1naw by marrying the daughter of the Añūṟṟuva-veḷāṉ.

Taking these nine persons, they are bound to beat the drums for the three daily sandhis and at ardayāmam and paḷḷiyeḻucci.

The land given to them: taking the land at the western portion of the dry land devadānam in our village, named Perumāḷvati... to beat the drums as long as the moon and the sun last, I gave this, having executed it as Cempaṉ Aruḷan Nuttamaniti, known as Uttamacoḻa-muventaveḷār, the devotee of Śivakāmi. This is the signature of Sivakāmi Dharmapriyaṉ.

The land assigned specifically for paḷḷiyeḻucci within the dry land given to them, according to the tax assessment, is one mākāṇi.

These comprised copper-vessels for the sacred bath of the deity presented in the 4th year of Uttama-chōḷa by queen-mother Parāntakaṉ-Mādēviyār, a golden vessel (koḷgai) set with gems presented by her in the 6th year of the same king, a golden pot for pinnacle over the temple presented by her in the 3rd year of Rājakēsarivarman, evidently Rājarāja I; another set of rich presents made in the same year by the same lady, consisting of a golden image of Chandraśēkharadēva with a gold-plated copper pedestal and silver aureola and ornaments set with gems, besides a silver plate for offerings to the same deity; a silver pot and some gold ornaments by Sōrabbaiyār Tribhuvanamādēviyār, the queen of Uttama-chōḷa presented in the same year, and a gold flower by the same queen presented in that year in lieu of land gift for the Śivaśrāddha of her husband; some gold ornaments made with money presented to the temple by Parakēsarivarman (evidently Uttama-chōḷa himself) in his 10th and 11th years; a gold plate (paṭṭam) presented in the 4th year of Uttama-chōḷa by Kōyiṟpiḷḷaiyār to the god, two lamp stands by Parāntakaṉ-Mādēvi and two by Madhurāntaka (king); lastly 400 kāśu given by Parāntakaṉ-Mādēvi in the 2nd year of (her husband) Gaṇḍarāditya alias Mummaḍi-chōḷadēva towards the saṅkrānti bath of the deity every month and which was now in the 6th year of Rājakēsarivarman, converted into a land endowment by the assembly of Nāṅgūr. At the end is recorded another gift of 125 kaḻañju presented by the same queen for feeding a brāhmaṇa in the temple for the merit of her servant (aḍiyāḷ) Ilaichchiyan Maḻapāḍi, for which the assembly sold a land to her for endowment.

SII_translation:
Hail Prosperity! In the 6th year of king Rājakesarivarman, the record of the works and endowments made by Śrī Cempiyaṉmāteviyār—who was the queen of Śrī Kaṇṭarātittadēvar, the mother (taṅkaḷācciyār) of Śrī Uttamacoḻadēvar, and the daughter of the Maḻavaraiyar—to the god of Tiruveṇkāṭu is as follows:

In the 4th year of Śrī Uttamacoḻadēvar, she gave for ceremonial bathing (snapaṉam) 116 copper kalacams, 1 copper pot (kuṭam), 1 copper karakam, and 118 covering copper lids (mūṭac ceppakal). The total collective weight of all these, weighed with the silver balance of this temple, was 2,448 palam.

To the same god, in the 6th year, the gold coin endowment given by this same queen had a weight of 1,500 kaḻañcu. Set upon this, on the cikaṟam and across the four faces, were 5 rubies, 52 diamonds, and 3,261 pearls.

In the 3rd year of king Rājakesarivarman, she who is the glorious Cempiya1n-mātevi, daughter of the Ciraḻar Maḻavarkon, presented a golden pot (poiñpoṟkuṭam) weighing 1,500 kaḻañcu to be kept upon the sacred temple of Veṇkāṭar.

In the same year, the bronze image of Candraśēkhara placed in this temple weighed 4,998 three-quarters kaḻañcu. The gold leaf plated over the copper base for this same god, including the four māṇis, weighed 111 kaḻañcu. The gold leaf plated over the two panmatas made of copper for this same god weighed 29 three-quarters kaḻañcu with rubies. The silver prabhai made for this same god weighed 286 kaḻañcu and 3 mañcāṭis, and the gold plated over it weighed 159 quarter kaḻañcu. The ornaments made for this same god—two kuppis, one uḻuttu, one īraṇai, and one vāḷi—had a gold weight of 2 kaḻañcus, 5 pearls, 2 ēkāvalli necklaces, 28 pearls, 2 corals, 2 rājāvantam, 1 ruby necklace weighing 9 kaḻañcus, with 6 rubies set upon it, 36 crystal-set beads, 232 diamonds, 38 pearls, 21 emeralds, 1 golden forehead plaque (tāṇicca paṭṭikai) for the eye (nēttiram) weighing 5 kaḻañcus, with 1 ruby, 19 crystal rubies, 10 crystal diamonds, 3 pottis, and 272 pearls. The armlets (bhāhuvalayam) of this god weighed 92 [kaḻañcus]. One white chowrie (veṇcāmarai) with a hand portion weighing 31 kaḻañcus and 1 mañcāṭi, and a two-handed copper pedestal weighing 150 palam.

In the same year, a single golden flower given weighed 3 kaḻañcus and a half. For the Candraśēkharapperumāḷ brought and consecrated by her in the same year, one silver plate (taḷikai) given for food offerings weighed 351 kaḻañcus.

In the same year, the queen of Śrī Uttamacoḻadēvar, Ceṭṭaṉ Corappaiyār, also known as Tribhuvanamāteviyār, gave one silver kalaca-pāṉai weighing 27 palam, alongside one copper foot-washing vessel (kaṟikkāl) given by her. A golden flower given by her in the same year weighed 2 kaḻañcus, half, and a quarter. In the same year, for the Lord's performance of the śivaśrāddha, a golden flower given as land purchase value weighed 4 kaḻañcus, three-quarters, and 2 mañcāṭis.

In the 10th year of Kopparakesarivarman, 23 golden flowers made from coins exchanged (kācumāṟi) for the Lord's ornaments and flowers, when weighed together with the pearl beads obtained from the temple treasury, totaled 181 kaḻañcus. A tāli and tāli-cord made for the queen from coins similarly exchanged by her weighed 5 kaḻañcus.

In the 11th year, one paḷḷittoṅkal given, including one brass boss (moṭṭu), one paṟaḷai, and palm-leaf strips, had a gold weight of 40 kaḻañcus.

In the 4th year of Śrī Uttamacoḻadēvar, the temple child (koyirpiḷḷaiyār) gave a golden diadem (paṭṭam) for this god weighing 4 kaḻañcus, 8 mañcāṭis, and a kuḻi. For this same god, Parāntakan Mātevi gave two standing brass lamps (tarānilaiviḷakku), one measuring 7 cāṇ in height and one measuring 6 cāṇ. For this same god, Kaṇṭan Maturāntakaḻan, also known as Śrī Uttamacoḻadēvar, gave two standing brass lamps, one measuring 7 cāṇ and one measuring 6 cāṇ.

In the 6th year of king Rājakesarivarman, the assembly (sabhaiyom) of Nāṅkūr in Nāṅkūr nāṭu [recorded that] Śrī Cempiyaṉmāteviyār—who is Parāntakan Mātevaṭikaḷār, the daughter of the Maḻavaraiyar, who was the queen of Śrī Kaṇṭarātittadēvar and the mother of Śrī Uttamacoḻadēvar—[provided funds] for performing the monthly saṅkrānti snapa1nam for Śrī Tiruveṇkāṭatēvar, who is Śrī Kaṇṭarātittadēvar [also called] Śrī Mummuṭiccoḻadēvar, for the 2nd year. Since the assembly itself took the 400 kācus thus provided as they had not executed the land purchase, the assembly sold the land in the southern hamlet (teṉpiṭākai) for these kācus. The boundaries of this land are:
To the east, east of the assembly's land;
To the south, south of the large flower garden named after Cempiyaṉmātevi which was caused to be cooked/prepared by the Lord;
To the east of this same flower garden...
[The remaining lines detail additional boundaries, specific land measurements totaling fractions of māvus, payments made by the assembly under the supervision of the queen and temple officials, and signatures of witnesses including Tevaṉ Tāḻi Iśvaraṉ and the writer from Nāṅkūr.]

The assembly of Nāṅgūr received the amount and sold to the temple tax-free, one vēli of land for this purpose. Among the boundaries of the land mentioned, are a high road leading to Paṭṭaṉam (Kāvērippūmpaṭṭiṉam), and another land which had been endowed to the temple by a certain Kottappichchōḻar (Pottapi-Chōḷa). This person may be identical with the chief Pottappichchōḻar Śattiyaraiyar figuring in a record from Vṛiddhāchalam in the South Arcot district (No. 49 of 1918), dated in the 7th year of Rājarāja I, and hence the present inscription may be assigned to that king. SII_translation:
Hail Prosperity! In the fourth year of Kopparakesarivarman, for the god graciously residing at Tiruveṇkāṭu, Iraṉṉam Caṭṭi... and ... who tied ... at the mill ..., gave ... gold ... five at the mill. He is Ālamattāṉ, also known as Kaliyuga...śvaraṉ, a kaikkoḷan.

The temple executives (deva-kaḻmikaḷ) decreed and gave [the following instructions]: having cleared and reclaimed this land and taken possession of it, by raising water with the lift (eṟṟaṭai), he shall be permitted to perform his charitable act (tanmam) in this temple.

Having cleared this land beautifully, thirty kalams of paddy yielded by his prior cultivation through the lift, along with four kalams and a tūṇi of paddy to be measured out by him directly—making a total of thirty-four kalams and a tūṇi of paddy—shall be measured out according to the rājakesari standard.

As granted by Nallāvūr Āntai for... Kecan to endure as long as the moon and the sun last, the paddy according to this agreement shall be measured into the treasury of the Lord. For the sacred rice dish (caṭṭi-coṟu) established by him, at the rate of four nāḻis of paddy by the rājakesari standard for each of the two pots of caṭṭi-coṟu—making a kuruṇi of paddy for the two pots of caṭṭi-coṟu—the total for three hundred sixty days shall be thirty kalams of paddy.

We, the temple executives, are bound to cause this endowment to be paid annually as long as the moon and the sun last.

This is written by Kala-maṉ, the paraṭai-kāviti and accountant (karaṇattān) of Talaiccaṅkāṭu.

SII_notes: The inscription is partly built in. It records a sale of land by the nagarattār (merchant guild) of Ulagamādēvipuram in Ōymā-nāḍu to Gaṅgaṉ Ambalavaṉ Gaṇḍarādi[tta]śōḻa-Viḻuppaṟaiyaṉ of Kuvaḷālam (Kolar) in Gaṅgarusāyira province, who endowed it for a flower-garden for the temple. This donor is evidently identical with Ambalavaṉ Gaṇḍarādittaṉār who is referred to in No. 54 above of the 3rd year of Rājakēsarivarman, as belonging to the Perundaram of the king and as having constructed the temple. Like No. 54 this may also be assigned to Rājarāja I. Among the boundaries of the land is mentioned a ridge or pathway called Kalikaṇṭaka-peruvarambu.

SII_translation:
Hail Prosperity! In the 3rd year of king Rājakesarivarman, in the independent village (taṉiyūr) of Ulokamātēvipuram in Oymāṉāṭu, Ampalavaṉ Kaṇṭarātittaṉ of the Peruntaram class caused the stone temple (tirukkaṟṟaḷi) to be built for the supreme lord (paramasvāmikaḷ) of the sacred Kailāsa temple.

He gave ninety-six sheep for one perpetual lamp (nuntā viḷakku) [to be maintained] for this lamp to endure as long as the moon and the sun last.

May this charity... upon [our] heads. Do not forget righteousness (aṟam). There is no other companion except righteousness.

SII_translation:
Hail Prosperity! In the 10th year of Parakesarivarman, in the brahmadēyam of Kiḷinallūr in Ōymānāṭu, Parāśaṟan Tāyaṉ Cāttaṉ, among the governing assembly (āḷum-kaṇam) of this village, undertook to provide sacred food offerings (tiruvamutu) for the Lord of Tiruva[gni]śvaram: four nāḻis of rice on the new moon day (amāvāsi uvā) and four nāḻis of rice on every saṅkrānti. They shall also provide offerings daily across four divisions and three sandhis.

In this manner, the custodians of the sacred temple are to carry this out, as established by Parāśaṟan Tāyaṉ Cāttaṉ.

Those who protect this charity [shall receive the dust] of the sacred feet.

SII_translation:
Hail Prosperity! In the eighteenth year of king Rājakesarivarman, the manner in which we, the assembly of Kiḷiñalūr in Oymānāṭu, gave an agreement (oṭṭu) to Nāṭṭupperumāṉ, son of Vaḻutaikkāviti Vallirumpin of Vaḻutavūr in Vaḻutavūrnāṭu:

Having received seventy-five kaḻañcus of gold, we shall feed five brāhmaṇas daily. The manner of feeding is: two curries, and one uḻakku of ghee daily for the five persons, served as a meal without fail. We shall feed guests, visitors (atitikaḷ), and students (abhyāsikaḷ) without interruption.

Having taken this gold, we, the assembly of Kiḷiñalūr, have given this agreement such that if anyone fails in this manner, they shall pay a daily judicial fine starting from eight [kasus] as prescribed by the seat of justice (dharmmāsanam). Furthermore, we agreed to provide five portions of rice daily to the temple there.

For the seventy-five kaḻañcus of gold, as interest, we, the assembly of Kiḷiñalūr, shall feed the five persons without fail, subject to the half-fine (araiyataṇṭam) and full fine (teva-taṇṭam). We stood firmly committed to this sacred place (talam). Those who plot evil against this village shall incur sin.

SII_translation:
Hail Prosperity! In the 16th year of Parakesarivarman, we, the mahāsabhai of Kiḷinalūr in Oymānāṭu, [sold land] to Cāttaṉ Kallaṭikaḷ of Veṣālipāṭi... Puṭaipākkamuṭaiyāṉ.

The agreement for the wet land where paddy grew in our village, according to the expanded terms, is to measure out one tūṇi of paddy per ceṟu from our village tank every year, following the floral path (pūvaḻi), to endure as long as the moon and the sun last. Having taken the price in dravya from this Cāttaṉ Mallaṭikaḷ... for this tank... we sold it for the benefit of Cātta0n Mallaṭikaḷ and engraved and gave the stone inscription (śilālaikhai)...

[An amount of] ... kaḻañcus of gold is to serve as the maṉṟu for the temple there (aṉṟāḷ koil), and this maṉṟu... In this manner, this charity... sold for Cāttaṉ Mallaṭikaḷ... we, the mahāsabhai.
